lead.headline: Night tone logged as 'louder' for the tenth night; 640 calls to the Exchange
lead.deck: Queens Exchange's sheets enter the same word on every night since October 6; Dr. Rastin's readings 'above before'; Queens Light & Power refers callers to its statement of Monday
lead.body: The Queens Exchange logged 640 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. today reporting the tone, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states, the operators entering it as 'louder' for the tenth night in succession. Dr. Emil Rastin states that his readings on the Corona roof were 'above before' at each hour. Mr. Victor Ashby, for Queens Light & Power, referred inquiries to the company's statement of Monday. In Sunnyside, the Police Department states, a householder was asked at 2:40 a.m. to take her bed in from the stoop.

columns.headline: Professor Fisher tells purchasing agents prices stand on a 'high plateau'
columns.body: Professor Irving Fisher of Yale told the Purchasing Agents Association last night that stock prices stand at 'what looks like a permanently high plateau,' the association states. The address, of 31 minutes, was recorded by the club's system and will be printed by the association.

columns.headline: Stocks ease to 345.6 on 3,630,000 shares; tone book enters 'held'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange eased yesterday on a volume of 3,630,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 345.6, a loss of 1.6. The ticker ran 12 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'held.'

columns.headline: Senate vault's record of March 27 unclaimed in its thirtieth week
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27 containing the word 'resent' remains unclaimed in the vault at Albany in its thirtieth week. Senator Rufus Keel's secretary states that the Senator 'has nothing to send.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 60. Wednesday. Ten nights louder. Earmuffs at the Arcade, 40 cents.

lead.headline: Ten nights of the Hum, and the light company answers in a monotone
lead.deck: Six hundred and forty calls before dawn and 'louder' on every sheet; Mr. Ashby refers the borough to Monday's statement, which refers the borough to nothing
lead.body: Ten nights running the girls at the Queens Exchange have written 'louder' on the night sheet, and last night six hundred and forty people rang to say so. Queens Light & Power's Mr. Ashby, asked for a word, gave the same one as Monday, which was 'not.' The Sunnyside lady who moved her bed to the stoop was asked by a patrolman at twenty to three to move it back in. She did. She says the Hum came in with her. She has asked the patrolman to take it outside.

columns.headline: Professor Fisher calls it a high plateau, and the ticker holds the note
columns.body: Professor Fisher of Yale told the purchasing agents last night that stocks stand on a permanently high plateau, and the ticker, twelve minutes behind as usual, held its note. The Jamaica dentist has had the speech read to him twice. He says a plateau is a thing with edges.

columns.headline: Week thirty: the Senator has 'nothing to send,' and sends that
columns.body: Thirty weeks in the vault for 'resent.' The Senator's secretary told Mr. Pratt yesterday that the Senator has nothing to send. Mr. Pratt asked if he might file that. She said it was not a message. He has filed it under not a message.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can you put me through to the Hum?'
columns.body: Madam, there is no number for it. Several readers have asked the night girls to connect them, and one girl did plug a caller into an empty jack to oblige. The caller said, 'Yes, that's it.' The supervisor has asked her not to do that again.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Barclay 4420 not rung today by anybody, the Queens Exchange says, and the Speaker's man with the nickel has been told to save it.

lead.headline: Appellate Division grants the Board leave to take the Riverhead seconds up
lead.deck: Motion granted without opinion at 11 a.m.; the appeal to be heard in the Court of Appeals' January term; the 11 seconds to remain sealed meanwhile; Mr. Gorman states that he expected it
lead.body: The Appellate Division, Second Department, yesterday granted the Board of Elections leave to appeal to the Court of Appeals against the order of September 23 unsealing 11 seconds of the Riverhead record of January 3, the clerk states. No opinion was given. The appeal will be heard in the January term. The 11 seconds remain sealed. Chairman Delaney stated that the Board was 'gratified on behalf of the wire.' Mr. Francis Gorman stated that he had expected it and would go to Albany 'on the first train.'

columns.headline: Stocks fall 9.5 points to 336.1 on 4,090,000 shares; ticker 25 minutes late
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange fell yesterday on a volume of 4,090,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 336.1, a loss of 9.5. The ticker ran 25 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'low.'

columns.headline: Radio Division's Maspeth watch in its fourth week; nothing heard
columns.body: Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division states that the Maspeth watch, in its fourth week, has heard nothing since the earpiece was replaced on October 5. He states that the watch will be reviewed on Saturday. WORS 1610 has not been heard on it since September 25.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society fixes Tuesday for comparing the window records
columns.body: Mr. Linus Fahey of the Phonautograph Society of Queens states that the seven records taken at a Long Island City window and the boy's two will be compared at its rooms at 8 p.m. on Tuesday. The boy's request to sit outside the door has been granted.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Exchange states 668 calls reporting the tone between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. today, the operators entering 'louder.'

speaker.ear: Cloudy. High 58. Thursday. Nine points down. The dentist is listening.

lead.headline: Gorman's seconds get a long-distance call: Albany will take it in January
lead.deck: The Appellate Division says yes to the Board without saying why, the eleven Riverhead seconds go back on hold for the winter, and Mr. Gorman checks the train times
lead.body: Eleven seconds of a Riverhead room, sealed since January, were to be played this autumn in a judge's chambers. Now they will be argued over in Albany in January instead, the Appellate Division having given the Board of Elections leave to appeal, without a word of reasons. Chairman Delaney says the Board is gratified on behalf of the wire. The wire has not been asked. Mr. Gorman says he expected it and has bought a timetable. He says the seconds will keep. They have kept so far.

columns.headline: The Street drops nine, and the ticker's delivery runs twenty-five minutes late
columns.body: Down nine and a half yesterday on four million shares, and the ticker read the closing prices twenty-five minutes after the closing. The Jamaica dentist, asked at his chair, said, 'Open wider.' The Flushing undertaker has stopped taking notes at his broker's and now only listens.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Pike's Maspeth men listen four weeks to a hung-up line
columns.body: Four weeks on the Maspeth baker's line, twelve days of it hung up, and Mr. Pike's men have heard a hung-up line hum a little and nothing else. Mr. Pike will review the watch on Saturday. The men have asked for a review of the chairs.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Jackson Heights gets engaged by long distance
columns.body: Darlings, a Jackson Heights girl was engaged on Sunday to a young man in Chicago by long distance, her mother and his on the same line, both saying yes before the couple could. The Chicago operator says it took four minutes and much crying, mostly the mothers'.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Long Island City, seven o'clock: the boy whose window was recorded has been seen on his stoop, practising sitting still outside a door.

lead.headline: Justice Hallam asks Mr. Crane's office who made the primary records
lead.deck: Court directs an affidavit by Monday stating 'by whom or by what' the 23 districts' records were made; decision on Mr. Feeney's application remains reserved
lead.body: Justice Moses Hallam yesterday directed Mr. Hollis Crane's office to file by Monday an affidavit stating 'by whom or by what' the records of the 23 disputed primary districts of June 4 were made, the clerk of the Supreme Court at Long Island City states. The direction follows the statement of Mr. Lowell Tibbs, for the office, that it 'holds what it did not make.' Decision on Alderman John Feeney's application remains reserved. Mr. Feeney stated that the question was 'the right one, at last.'

columns.headline: Stocks rise 5.8 to 341.9 on 3,860,000 shares; tone book enters 'even'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 3,860,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 341.9, a gain of 5.8. The ticker ran 18 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'even.'

columns.headline: Mr. Crane's letter to Buffalo held at General Delivery, uncalled for
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane's office states that its letter of October 7 to Mr. Royal Haskin, addressed to General Delivery at Buffalo for want of a street, has been held there ten days uncalled for, the Buffalo postmaster states. The seal on the Ditmars Avenue room remains.

columns.headline: Astoria Ice Company takes on 38 drivers for the winter round
columns.body: The Astoria Ice Company states that it has taken on 38 drivers and 41 horses for the winter round, the horses bought at the Jamaica sale on Tuesday at an average of 92 dollars. Its motor wagons will be laid up on November 1. Coal deliveries begin Monday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Showers. High 61. Friday. Twenty-nine Fridays. Bring an umbrella for the cat.

lead.headline: Party Line holds the line at Position 12 for a twenty-ninth Friday
lead.deck: No tin from Corona again; the Exchange cat goes straight past the parcel window to her chair at Position 12, and the night girl takes her calls round her
lead.body: Twenty-nine Fridays now since the last tin came from Corona, and this afternoon Party Line did not even wait at the parcel window. She looked at it at four, as at an old friend across the street, and went straight on to Position 12 and the spare chair. The night girl came on at six and took her calls round her, reaching over. At eleven the cat woke once, at a Long Island call, and went back to sleep. The supervisor has given up noting the chair.

columns.headline: Judge Hallam asks who cut the primary records, and Crane's office must say
columns.body: Justice Hallam wants an affidavit by Monday saying by whom or by what the twenty-three primary records were made. The 'or by what' is his own. Mr. Feeney says it is the right question at last. Mr. Crane's office has not said whether it has the right answer.

columns.headline: Mr. Crane writes to Buffalo, and his letter is left on hold
columns.body: Mr. Crane wrote to Mr. Haskin at Buffalo, General Delivery, having no street, and ten days later the letter is still in the pigeonhole. The Buffalo postmaster says it is safe. The Ditmars Avenue room stays sealed. It is the only party to this that is not travelling.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'My husband rings his broker every hour. Should I listen?'
columns.body: Madam, the operator listens so you need not. She says your husband asks the same question every hour and gets a longer answer each time. She recommends a good supper and no calls after four. The broker, she says, would recommend the same, if he could get off the line.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Exchange, ten o'clock: Party Line asleep at 12; the night girl has put a cushion on the switchboard shelf. The supervisor pretended not to see it.

lead.headline: Week's count: 4,402 night calls on the tone, 'louder' on all seven nights
lead.deck: Highest weekly count since February; thirteen nights 'louder' in succession; Dr. Rastin's Corona readings 'above before'; Brooklyn door at 1,904; Queens Light & Power declines to add to its statement
lead.body: The Queens Exchange logged 4,402 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting the tone, against 3,904, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states, the highest weekly count since February. The operators' sheets enter it as 'louder' on each night, the thirteenth such night in succession. Dr. Emil Rastin states that his Corona readings are 'above before.' The Brooklyn Exchange's door shows 1,904. Queens Light & Power declined to add to its statement of Monday.

columns.headline: Stocks fall 8.6 to 333.3 on 3,500,000 shares; ticker 33 minutes late
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange fell yesterday on a volume of 3,500,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 333.3, a loss of 8.6. The ticker ran 33 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'dropped.'

columns.headline: Privy Council rules that women are 'persons' for the Canadian Senate
columns.body: The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council ruled in London yesterday that women are 'persons' within the meaning of the British North America Act and may be summoned to the Canadian Senate, the Canadian Press states. The judgment was read in 14 minutes and cabled to Ottawa in full.

columns.headline: No parcel for Position 43 on a twenty-ninth Friday
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the twenty-ninth Friday without one, the supervisor states. The animal did not stop at the parcel window, passing it at 4 p.m., and slept at Position 12 until the morning shift.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Radio Division ends its watch on the Maspeth line at noon today after 23 days, Mr. Harold Pike states; nothing was heard.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 57. Saturday. Ten points in two hours. The short session felt long.

lead.headline: Two hours, ten points: the Street's Saturday matinee gets the hook
lead.deck: The Exchange's half-day falls nine and a half points by noon on three and a half million shares, and the brokers spend the afternoon on the telephone to Queens
lead.body: Saturday is the Exchange's short session, two hours, and this morning it was long enough. The average fell nine and a half points by noon on three and a half million shares, a full day's business done in a hurry. The ticker was twenty minutes late, and the brokers did not wait for it. By one o'clock they were on the telephone to their customers in Queens, asking for more money by Monday. The Jamaica dentist was asked. He has gone to the pictures.

columns.headline: The Hum runs up its biggest bill, and the light company won't take the charges
columns.body: Four thousand four hundred and two calls this week about the night tone, thirteen nights 'louder' in a row, and Queens Light & Power has nothing to add. In Astoria a man has nailed a second blanket over his point. He says the first one has started humming too.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: London rules ladies are persons, and Ottawa takes the call
columns.body: Darlings, the Privy Council has ruled that Canadian women are persons and may sit in the Senate at Ottawa. The judgment was cabled whole. The Listening Lady has always known she was a person, having been told so by every operator in Queens, in a whisper.

columns.headline: 'Danko, dog' sits through the fire drill, and P.S. 11's register rings true
columns.body: The terrier on P.S. 11's register answered the roll all week and on Thursday led the fire drill. Mrs. Fitch says he is hers. Dr. Voight says he is his. Mrs. Ahl says he is the school's. He goes home, nightly, to none of them.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Maspeth, noon: Mr. Pike's men packed up their headsets and went home. The baker gave them a loaf each. Nothing heard, the report says.

editorial.headline: Sound as a bell, says Mr. Fenn, and a bell rings
editorial.body: Mr. Lucius Fenn returned from his travels on Tuesday and told the shareholders of his Trust, at the Elks' Hall, that the market is as sound as a church bell. At that moment every church bell in Long Island City began to ring, forty-one times each, which is the number of widows who had come to the hall to ask for their money and been told to wait. The ringers were found to be the borough's laundresses, operators and stenographers, who had been given the keys to the belfries by persons unknown. This newspaper deplores the misuse of a sacred instrument. We note that every one of the forty-one widows was paid before the bells stopped.

lead.headline: Stocks fall 9.4 to 323.9 at Saturday's session; brokers' calls fill the day
lead.deck: 3,490,000 shares in two hours; ticker 20 minutes late; Queens Exchange puts through 2,310 calls from Manhattan brokers' offices between noon and 6 p.m.; tone book enters 'dropped'
lead.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange fell at yesterday's two-hour session on a volume of 3,490,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 323.9, a loss of 9.4, the Exchange states. The ticker ran 20 minutes late. The tone book records its tone at noon as 'dropped.' The Queens Exchange states that it put through 2,310 calls from brokers' offices in Manhattan to Queens subscribers between noon and 6 p.m., against 410 on the Saturday before. Several brokers' offices will be open today.

columns.headline: Light's Golden Jubilee at Dearborn tomorrow; Queens street lamps to mark it
columns.body: Mr. Thomas A. Edison will re-enact the lighting of his first lamp of 1879 at Dearborn, Michigan, tomorrow evening before President Hoover and Mr. Henry Ford, the Jubilee committee states. Queens Light & Power states that the borough's street lamps will be switched off and on at the moment.

columns.headline: Byrd expedition reports the geological party ready to start south
columns.body: Commander Richard E. Byrd's expedition states by wire that the geological party under Dr. Laurence Gould will start south 'within the fortnight' and that the temperature at Little America was 14 degrees below zero on Friday. The message concerned dogs.

columns.headline: Radio Division ends its Maspeth watch after 23 days; nothing heard
columns.body: Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division states that the watch on the Maspeth subscriber's line was ended at noon yesterday after 23 days, nothing having been heard. Mr. Anton Ruzicka, the subscriber, states that he was not consulted on either its beginning or its end.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 55. Sunday. The brokers are working. Lock the door.

lead.headline: Mr. Edison's bright idea turns fifty, and the light company takes its cue
lead.deck: Tomorrow night at Dearborn the old man lights the lamp again for the President and Mr. Ford, and Queens Light & Power promises to blink every street lamp in the borough on the signal
lead.body: Fifty years ago Mr. Edison got a lamp to burn for forty hours, and tomorrow night at Dearborn he will do it again for President Hoover and Mr. Ford, by wire to the nation. Queens Light & Power will switch the borough's street lamps off and on at the moment, a thing it has never done for anybody. It is the first time the company has admitted to a signal. The Speaker will be on Jackson Avenue, watching for the blink and listening for the Hum.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Mr. Pike's men hang up on Maspeth after twenty-three days
columns.body: The Radio Division's watch on the Maspeth line ended yesterday at noon, twenty-three days, nothing heard. The office boy took the Maspeth pin out of his map and found the hole would not close. He has put the pin back. Mr. Pike has not asked him why.

columns.headline: The brokers keep Sunday on the line, and the Sabbath gets a wrong number
columns.body: Wall Street offices are open today, a Sunday, blinds down. The Queens Exchange has put on four extra girls. One of them asked a broker's man if he knew it was Sunday. He said he knew what day it was, he just did not know what price.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will the light company really blink for Mr. Edison?'
columns.body: Sir, it says so. The night girls at the Queens Exchange have asked to be told the moment, so that they can look out of the window. The supervisor says that is not their job. The supervisor has also asked to be told.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Port Washington, two o'clock this morning: Mr. Brewer's cat turned her back on the Sound again. He has started setting his alarm to watch.

lead.headline: Newtown High beats Jamaica High 13 to 6 at Dexter Park; clock upheld
lead.deck: Queens schoolboy game decided with 40 seconds to play; the League hears the park's record of the fourth period and finds the clock right by 3 seconds; Bayside and Flushing meet Saturday
lead.body: Newtown High School defeated Jamaica High School 13 to 6 at Dexter Park, Woodhaven, on Saturday before about 4,100, the Public Schools Athletic League states. Newtown scored its second touchdown in the fourth period with 40 seconds to play. Jamaica's coach, Mr. Arthur Dodd, disputed the clock. The League heard the park's record of the period in its office at 9 p.m. and found the clock right by 3 seconds. Bayside and Flushing meet at Dexter Park on Saturday.

columns.headline: Light's Golden Jubilee tonight; Queens lamps to go off at Mr. Edison's signal
columns.body: President Hoover arrived at Dearborn, Michigan, yesterday for tonight's Light's Golden Jubilee, at which Mr. Thomas A. Edison re-enacts the lighting of his lamp of 1879. Queens Light & Power states that its street lamps will be switched off at the signal and on again after one minute.

columns.headline: Brokers' calls to Queens on Sunday put at 1,880 by the Exchange
columns.body: The Queens Exchange states that it put through 1,880 calls from brokers' offices in Manhattan to Queens subscribers yesterday, a Sunday, between 10 a.m. and 8 p.m. Four operators were brought in. Superintendent Wilfred Arne states that the Exchange 'will staff to the calls.'

columns.headline: Valve prices unchanged at six for a dollar; Newark output 'full'
columns.body: Retail valve prices in Queens were unchanged last week at six for a dollar, the Queens Radio Dealers' Association states, eggs at 52 cents the dozen. The Newark works state that output is 'full' and that stocks held by the jobbers are 'ample.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Barclay 4420 was not rung last week, the Queens Exchange states, Mr. Ewald having asked that it not be.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 56. Monday. Six million shares. The ticker kept its own time.

lead.headline: Six million shares and the ticker an hour behind: the Street sells by ear
lead.deck: The heaviest Monday of the year leaves the tape sixty-four minutes late at the bell, brokers trade on what they hear down the hall, and then the old man at Dearborn lights his lamp
lead.body: Six million and ninety thousand shares changed hands on the Exchange today, and by the closing bell the ticker was sixty-four minutes behind them. For an hour the brokers bought and sold on what the man beside them said, which is how the Speaker gets its news too, and we are not proud of it. The average finished down three, not so bad as the morning sounded. At eight tonight Mr. Edison lights his lamp at Dearborn. Somebody should hand him the ticker.

columns.headline: Newtown wins with forty seconds left, and the League plays back the clock
columns.body: Jamaica's coach said the clock was fast, so the Schools League sat down at nine on Saturday night and listened to the whole fourth period. The clock was right by three seconds. The coach asked to hear it again. The League said it had heard enough football for one night.

columns.headline: 'Danko, dog' barks the answer to the sums, and P.S. 11 records a three
columns.body: Miss Varick at P.S. 11 asked what one and two made, and the terrier barked three times before anyone else answered. The system has entered it. Mrs. Fitch says he is clever because he is hers. Dr. Voight says it was an accident. Mrs. Ahl was not consulted.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Why do the brokers ring on Sunday?'
columns.body: Sir, because the market fell on Saturday and they want more money before it opens. The operator puts them through. She does not read your bank book. She would add that a broker who rings on Sunday is a broker who did not sleep on Saturday, and you should.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Jackson Avenue, eight o'clock: the street lamps went out for one minute for Mr. Edison. In the dark the Hum came up the avenue plain as a tram. Then the lamps came on.

lead.headline: Mr. Edison re-lights his lamp at Dearborn; Queens street lamps out one minute
lead.deck: President Hoover and Mr. Ford present at the Jubilee; the re-enactment carried by wire to the nation; Queens Light & Power states its lamps went off at 7:52 p.m. and on at 7:53
lead.body: Mr. Thomas A. Edison re-enacted the lighting of his first incandescent lamp at Dearborn, Michigan, last night before President Hoover and Mr. Henry Ford, the Jubilee committee states. The occasion was carried by wire. Queens Light & Power states that the borough's street lamps were switched off at 7:52 p.m. and on at 7:53. The Queens Exchange states that it received 312 calls in that minute, of which 290 reported the tone. Mr. Edison, who is hard of hearing, did not hear the broadcast.

columns.headline: Stocks fall 3.0 to 320.9 on 6,090,000 shares; ticker 64 minutes late
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange fell yesterday on a volume of 6,090,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 320.9, a loss of 3.0. The ticker ran 64 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'low.'

columns.headline: Mr. Crane's office files its affidavit: the records 'made by the rooms'
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane's office filed its affidavit with Justice Moses Hallam at 4:10 p.m. yesterday stating that the 23 districts' records were 'made by the rooms in which the counting took place, the office having made none of them.' Decision remains reserved.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society compares the window records at 8 p.m. today
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens compares the seven records it took at a Long Island City window with the two from the boy's own recorder at its rooms at 8 p.m. today, Mr. Linus Fahey states. The comparison is private. The Society will issue a statement tomorrow.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 59. Tuesday. Up five. The boy waits by the door.

lead.headline: The boy sits by the Society's door, all ears, while nine records compare notes
lead.deck: Eight o'clock in the Phonautograph Society's rooms: seven records from the window, two from the boy's own machine, and a chair in the hall with a boy on it
lead.body: Tonight at eight the Phonautograph Society of Queens will play the nine records of a Long Island City window side by side: seven made by its own machine, between midnight and four, and two made by the boy who lives behind the window, on his own. The boy will be in the hall on a chair, the Society having said yes. His mother is coming with a flask of tea. Mr. Fahey says the result will be stated tomorrow and kept until 1978. The boy says tomorrow will do.

columns.headline: The ticker catches its breath, and the Street gets five points back on the line
columns.body: Up five and a half today on four million shares, and the ticker only twenty-two minutes behind, which counts as prompt these days. The brokers who rang Queens all Sunday rang again this afternoon to say not to worry. The dentist says that is the call that worries him.

columns.headline: Mr. Edison throws the switch, and Queens hears itself in the dark
columns.body: Last night at eight minutes to eight every street lamp in Queens went out for one minute for Mr. Edison. Two hundred and ninety people rang the Exchange in that minute about the Hum. The light company says the minute went exactly as planned. It did not say whose plan.

columns.headline: Crane's office swears it never touched the records: the rooms did the talking
columns.body: By whom or by what, asked Justice Hallam, were the primary records made? By the rooms, says Mr. Crane's affidavit, sworn and filed at ten past four. Mr. Feeney says that is an answer. The judge has reserved it with the rest. The rooms have not been asked to swear.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Long Island City, ten o'clock: the boy came out of the Society's hall and said nothing to the Speaker's man. His mother said he had heard enough for one night.

lead.headline: Phonautograph Society finds the nine window records agree but for 4 seconds
lead.deck: The boy's two records carry 4 seconds at 3:11 a.m. that the Society's seven do not; Mr. Fahey declines to describe them; all nine to be sealed for 1978
lead.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens compared the nine records taken at a Long Island City window at its rooms last night, Mr. Linus Fahey states, seven made by the Society's machine and two by the boy's own. All nine agree, Mr. Fahey states, except that the boy's two carry 4 seconds at 3:11 a.m. that the Society's seven do not. He declined to describe the 4 seconds. The nine records will be sealed for 1978. The boy waited in the hall for 1 hour 50 minutes.

columns.headline: Stocks rise 5.6 to 326.5 on 4,130,000 shares; tone book enters 'up'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 4,130,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 326.5, a gain of 5.6. The ticker ran 22 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'up.'

columns.headline: Senate vault's record of March 27 unclaimed in its thirty-first week
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27 containing the word 'resent' remains unclaimed in the vault at Albany in its thirty-first week. Senator Rufus Keel's secretary asked on Monday at what hours the vault is open. She was told.

columns.headline: Signal Ground Rents' box at the General Post Office emptied a third time
columns.body: The Post Office states that the box of Signal Ground Rents Inc. at the General Post Office was emptied on Monday by a person holding its key, the third time since September 21. The Municipal Court clerk still holds 2,060 dollars deposited for the company.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Exchange states 702 calls reporting the tone between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. today, the operators entering 'louder.'

speaker.ear: Cloudy. High 57. Wednesday. The last hour was the worst hour. Sit down for this.

lead.headline: The last hour drops off the line, and the Street falls twenty before supper
lead.deck: Two and a half million shares sold between two and three o'clock, the average down twenty and two-thirds, and the tape reading prices to an empty floor forty minutes after the bell
lead.body: It was a quiet day on the Exchange until two o'clock, and then it was not. In the last hour two and a half million shares were sold, more than some whole days this summer, and the average lost twenty points and more. The ticker, which had been doing well, fell forty minutes behind and was still reading prices when the floor had emptied. The brokers went home and the telephones did not. Queens rang Manhattan all evening. Manhattan, for once, was in.

columns.headline: The boy's record runs four seconds long, and the Society files them for 1978
columns.body: Nine records agree, says Mr. Fahey, except that the boy's two have four seconds at eleven past three that the Society's seven have not. He will not say what is on them. The boy waited nearly two hours. His mother says he slept all the way home.

columns.headline: Week thirty-one: the Senator's office rings the vault for its hours
columns.body: Thirty-one weeks in the vault for 'resent.' On Monday the Senator's secretary asked Mr. Pratt at what hours the vault is open. Ten to four, he said. She went upstairs. Mr. Pratt has stood at the vault door at ten every morning since.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Who keeps emptying the Arcade landlord's box?'
columns.body: Madam, the Post Office says a person with the key, which is what the Post Office always says. It is the third time. Mr. Ewald's two thousand and sixty dollars are still in the court clerk's second drawer. Nobody has come for them, by box, by wire, or by room.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Six o'clock: Wall Street lit up and talking to itself. The Speaker's man asked a broker's boy for a word. He gave two. We cannot print either.

record.ear: Extra edition, 1:45 p.m. Fair, cool. High 58. Low 44.

lead.headline: Stocks break at the opening; ticker 90 minutes behind the floor by noon
lead.deck: Heavy selling from 10 a.m.; the ticker 20 minutes late at 10:40 and 90 at noon; tone book enters 'broken' at 11:22; visitors' gallery closed; bankers meet at 23 Wall Street
lead.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange broke this morning under selling heavier than any in its history, the Exchange states. The ticker ran 20 minutes late at 10:40 a.m. and 90 minutes late at noon. At 11:22 a.m. the tone book entered 'broken,' the ticker's voice having 'gone up and not come down.' The gallery was closed at 12:30 p.m. and the floor's system carried to the street. Five bankers met at the offices of J. P. Morgan & Co. at noon.

columns.headline: Queens Exchange's calls to Manhattan 'beyond the board' from 10:15 a.m.
columns.body: The Queens Exchange states that calls from Queens to brokers' offices in Manhattan have been 'beyond the board' since 10:15 a.m., and that operators are instructed to place brokers' margin calls to Queens subscribers in the order received. Superintendent Wilfred Arne states that 'every position is staffed.'

columns.headline: Crowd of 4,000 at this newspaper's window on Jackson Avenue; trolleys stopped
columns.body: A crowd estimated by the Police Department at 4,000 has stood before this newspaper's window on Jackson Avenue since 11 a.m., hearing the floor by wire. Trolleys were stopped from 11:40 a.m. Mounted police were sent at noon. The crowd is orderly and very quiet.

columns.headline: Mr. Lamont states that there has been 'a little distressed selling'
columns.body: Mr. Thomas W. Lamont, of J. P. Morgan & Co., stated to the press at 1:10 p.m., after the bankers' meeting, that there had been 'a little distressed selling on the Stock Exchange,' owing to a technical condition of the market. Four other bankers were present.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: 1:30 p.m.: Mr. Richard Whitney bids 205 for 10,000 shares of Steel at its post; the bid was heard at this newspaper's window.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 58. Thursday. A black day downtown. Hold on to each other.

lead.headline: The ticker loses its voice, and Wall Street gets the busy signal all day
lead.deck: Thirteen million shares, prices falling faster than the tape can read them, the gallery shut and the floor heard through a wire; at noon five bankers pass the hat and the Street finds a floor
lead.body: At eleven this morning the ticker's voice broke. That is the clerk's word, not ours: it went up and did not come down. By noon it was ninety minutes behind, and brokers were selling on rumour, shouting into telephones that would not connect. The gallery was shut and the floor was heard through the wire instead. Then at half past one Mr. Whitney walked to the Steel post and bid 205, loud, and the Street steadied. The brokers will be counting till morning. Their customers will be counting longer.

columns.headline: Jackson Avenue holds the line: four thousand at the Record's window
columns.body: From eleven o'clock Jackson Avenue was full, four thousand people in front of the Record's window hearing the floor through the wire, and the Speaker's man never heard a crowd so quiet. When Whitney bid 205, somebody said 'there.' That was all.

columns.headline: The bankers pass the hat at 23 Wall Street, and the Street changes its tune
columns.body: Five bankers met at noon at the Morgan office, and at ten past one Mr. Lamont said there had been 'a little distressed selling.' We would like to hear him describe a lot. By two the tone had come up. The bankers had brought their own.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'My broker rang. What does he want?'
columns.body: Madam, he wants more money by tomorrow, and the operator is sorry she had to put him through. If you cannot pay him, ring your bank in the morning, not your broker tonight. The operator will be on. She is not going home.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Seven o'clock: the ticker read the day's last price at eight minutes past seven, four hours after the bell. Jackson Avenue stayed to hear it.

lead.headline: 12,894,650 shares sold; average closes at 299.5 after falling to 272.3
lead.deck: Heaviest day in the Exchange's history; bankers' support at 1:30 p.m. recovers most of the morning's loss; the ticker's last price read at 7:08 p.m.; the tone book's 'broken' left standing
lead.body: The Stock Exchange sold 12,894,650 shares yesterday, its most ever, the average falling to 272.3 by noon and closing at 299.5, a loss of 6.4, the Exchange states. The recovery followed Mr. Richard Whitney's bid of 205 for 10,000 shares of Steel at 1:30 p.m. for a group of bankers. The ticker read its last price at 7:08 p.m. The tone book made no entry after 'broken.' Mr. Winston Churchill was in the gallery.

columns.headline: Queens Exchange puts through 41,300 calls to Manhattan; 3,900 margin calls
columns.body: The Queens Exchange put through 41,300 calls between Queens and Manhattan yesterday, against 9,000 ordinarily, and placed 3,900 margin calls from brokers to Queens subscribers between noon and midnight. Where a broker could not hold, the operator read his message to the subscriber.

columns.headline: Crowd of 6,000 hears the floor at this newspaper's window until 7:30 p.m.
columns.body: The crowd before this newspaper's window on Jackson Avenue reached about 6,000 at 2 p.m., the Police Department states, and the last of it left at 7:30 p.m., after the ticker's final price. A terrier sat at the front from 11 a.m.

columns.headline: Barclay 4420 answered once at 2:14 p.m.; no word spoken; 46 seconds
columns.body: The Telephone Company states that every Barclay line was engaged yesterday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. except Barclay 4420, entered for Signal Ground Rents Inc. Rung once, at 2:14 p.m., it was answered. No word was spoken. The line cleared after 46 seconds.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Dealers in Jamaica report valves sold out at six for a dollar by 4 p.m. yesterday; buyers stated that they wished to hear the news sooner.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 56. Friday. Thirty Fridays. The Street is up. So was everyone, all night.

lead.headline: The bankers put the Street on hold, and for one Friday the hold holds
lead.deck: Six million shares and the average up two; the ticker on time by half past two; Mr. Hoover says business is sound; brokers sleep under their desks and their customers don't sleep at all
lead.body: After Thursday, Friday was quiet, and quiet sounded wonderful. The bankers who met at noon yesterday kept their money on the floor, and the average closed up two on six million shares. By half past two the ticker had caught up with the world, for the first time in a week. The President said business was sound. Brokers' clerks slept under their desks on Broad Street and worked the accounts through the night. In Queens the kitchen lamps stayed on late, over the bank books.

columns.headline: Mr. Hoover says business is sound, and the Speaker says sound is our business
columns.body: Mr. Hoover said today that the fundamental business of the country is on a sound and prosperous basis. The Speaker agrees that sound is fundamental, having sold nothing else since it started. We would add only that sound is what you hear when the ticker is ninety minutes late.

columns.headline: Party Line's thirtieth Friday, and she takes the long-distance shift at 12
columns.body: Thirty Fridays. Party Line passed the parcel window at four without stopping and went to Position 12, where the girl had put through four hundred margin calls on Thursday and cried twice. The cat sat in her lap all through the evening shift. No tin from Corona.

columns.headline: The only stock still rising: valves at the Arcade, sold out by four
columns.body: The only shares that went up all week were valves. News & Cigars at the Arcade sold its last six at a quarter to four yesterday, at a dollar ten, to a man who said he wanted the bad news before the Record had it. The Record's window was free.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Barclay 4420 picked up for somebody yesterday at fourteen minutes past two, the only line on the Barclay exchange that wasn't busy. Forty-six seconds, nothing said. Again.

lead.headline: Week's count: night calls on the tone fall to 2,118; two nights 'not taken'
lead.deck: Operators enter 'louder' on five nights; no entry for Thursday or Friday night, the night positions being given to brokers' calls; Dr. Rastin's readings 'above before'; Brooklyn door at 2,012
lead.body: The Queens Exchange logged 2,118 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting the tone, against 4,402, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The operators' sheets enter it as 'louder' on five nights and as 'not taken' on Thursday and Friday, the night positions being given to brokers' calls. Dr. Emil Rastin states that his Corona readings were 'above before' on each night, Thursday included. The Brooklyn Exchange's door shows 2,012. Queens Light & Power made no statement.

columns.headline: Stocks rise 1.7 to 301.2 on 5,920,000 shares; the President's statement
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 5,920,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 301.2, a gain of 1.7. President Hoover stated that the fundamental business of the country is 'on a sound and prosperous basis.'

columns.headline: No parcel for Position 43 on a thirtieth Friday
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the thirtieth Friday without one, the supervisor states. The animal passed the parcel window at 4 p.m. and remained at Position 12 through the evening shift.

columns.headline: Valves at a dollar ten the six in Queens; dealers report sales tripled
columns.body: The Queens Radio Dealers' Association states that valves sold at a dollar ten the six on Thursday and Friday, against a dollar, and that sales were three times the ordinary. Eggs were unchanged at 52 cents. The Newark works state that output will be raised on Monday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Albert B. Fall, former Secretary of the Interior, was found guilty at Washington yesterday of accepting a bribe, the court states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 58. Saturday. Short session. Long faces. Go to the park.

lead.headline: The Hum gets put on hold for the brokers, and keeps right on humming
lead.deck: Half the usual calls this week, not because the tone is quieter but because the night girls were putting through margin calls; Dr. Rastin's needle says 'above' on Thursday too
lead.body: Two thousand one hundred and eighteen calls about the night tone this week, half last week's, and the light company will be pleased until somebody tells it why. On Thursday and Friday nights the girls at the Queens Exchange had no time to write anything about the Hum. They were putting brokers through to kitchens in Corona and Woodhaven until two in the morning. Dr. Rastin was on his roof both nights. The Hum, he says, was the only thing in Queens that didn't change.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Must I answer when the broker rings at midnight?'
columns.body: Sir, you need not. The operator will tell him you are asleep, which is what she would like you to be. If he insists, she will take his message and read it to you at breakfast, over coffee, slowly. The Exchange has not ruled on it, but the girls have.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Forest Hills hangs up on the bridge club for a week
columns.body: Darlings, the Forest Hills ladies' bridge club, which plays by telephone, did not play this week. The party line was wanted for brokers. Mrs. Ormsby rang round on Friday to say they would play again when the husbands had stopped telephoning. The Listening Lady says that may be some time.

columns.headline: 'Danko, dog' keeps his ear to the window through the worst of it
columns.body: The P.S. 11 terrier sat at the front of the crowd at the Record's window from eleven on Thursday till half past seven. He did not bark at any price. Mrs. Fitch fetched him once, Dr. Voight twice. The Record printed him as 'a terrier.'

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Saturday's two hours: the average down two, the ticker on time, and on Broad Street a broker's clerk asleep on the kerb with his hat over his face. A patrolman let him be.

editorial.headline: The ticker stutters and the Editor stands firm
editorial.body: The market fell on Thursday harder and faster than the ticker's voice could tell it, the wire twenty minutes behind the panic, and brokers were heard on the floor rather than seen. Mr. Fenn's Widows' and Orphans' Trust has suspended withdrawals. This paper does not blame Mr. Fenn. We blame the woman called Lilith, who spread fear among the widows of Queens and caused them to withdraw their savings before the fall, thereby removing from the Trust exactly the money that would have been lost. That is to say, she has saved six hundred widows from ruin by unsettling the market. We cannot prove this was her intention. We are sure it was her fault.

lead.headline: Stocks ease 2.2 to 299.0 at Saturday's session; brokers' offices open today
lead.deck: 2,290,000 shares; ticker on time; brokers to ask customers for margin 'in good time for Monday'; Queens Exchange to staff 60 positions for brokers' calls
lead.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange eased at yesterday's two-hour session on a volume of 2,290,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 299.0, a loss of 2.2, the Exchange states. The ticker ran on time. The tone book records its tone at noon as 'held.' Brokers' offices in Manhattan will be open today to ask customers for margin 'in good time for Monday,' the Queens Exchange states, which will staff 60 positions for brokers' calls from 9 a.m.

columns.headline: Buffalo postmaster states Mr. Crane's letter called for on Friday
columns.body: The Buffalo postmaster states that Mr. Hollis Crane's letter to Mr. Royal Haskin, held at General Delivery since October 8, was called for at 4:40 p.m. on Friday by a person who signed for it as 'R. Haskin, for the property.' No reply has been received.

columns.headline: Thirty-one churches to switch off their systems for this morning's services
columns.body: The Queens Federation of Churches states that 31 Protestant churches in the borough will switch off their house systems for this morning's services 'at the request of the congregations,' the week's events being expected to be the subject of the sermons. The Federation gave no further reason.

columns.headline: Harbour master reports the hut cat facing inland at 2 a.m. for 15 nights
columns.body: Mr. Silas Brewer, harbour master at Port Washington, states that the cat kept in the hut lent last month to the Radio Division has turned at 2 a.m. to face away from the Sound on 15 nights in succession. The hut's receiver is not switched on.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 55. Sunday. The brokers are open. The churches are switched off.

lead.headline: Buffalo picks up Mr. Crane's letter, and still won't pick up the telephone
lead.deck: Twenty days at General Delivery and then, on Friday at twenty to five, a signature: 'R. Haskin, for the property'; no reply yet, no address, and the Ditmars room still under seal
lead.body: Mr. Crane's letter waited in a Buffalo pigeonhole for twenty days, and on Friday afternoon somebody came to the counter and asked for it. He signed 'R. Haskin, for the property.' The postmaster did not look up in time to say what he looked like. He says the man was tall, or else the counter was low. Mr. Crane has not had a reply. The Ditmars Avenue room is still sealed, and the property is still the property. Mr. Crane says he can wait. So, apparently, can it.

columns.headline: Thirty-one churches switch off, and the sermons go off the record
columns.body: This morning thirty-one Protestant churches in Queens switch their house systems off, at the congregations' request, so that what the ministers say about this week is heard once. The Speaker approves. Some things should be said to a room and not to the room's record.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Brewer's cat turns her back on the Sound a fifteenth night
columns.body: Fifteen nights now Sixteen-Ten the cat has woken at two at the Port Washington hut and turned round to face the land. Mr. Brewer sits up to watch. On Thursday she turned at two, and at half past turned again, and looked at the door.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Is the market open on Sunday?'
columns.body: Sir, the market is shut, but the brokers are open, which is not the same thing. Sixty girls at the Queens Exchange will be on today for their calls. If your broker rings, she will say so first, so that you may sit down.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Broad Street, noon: brokers' offices lit, blinds down, a boy with sandwiches going in and out. Nobody coming out with anything else.

lead.headline: Signal Ground Rents' box at the Post Office emptied a fourth time on Saturday
lead.deck: Mr. Ewald to deposit November's rent with the clerk on Friday; the court to hold 2,472 dollars; no word from the company in five months
lead.body: The Post Office states that the box of Signal Ground Rents Inc. at the General Post Office was emptied on Saturday by a person holding its key, the fourth time since September 21. Mr. Nathan Ewald stated that he will deposit the Vantry Arcade's November rent of 412 dollars with the clerk of the Municipal Court at 10 a.m. on Friday, the clerk then holding 2,472 dollars for the company. Mr. Ewald stated that his tenants had paid in full, 'every one, this week of all weeks.'

columns.headline: Bayside defeats Flushing 7 to 0 at Dexter Park; Newtown to meet Bayside
columns.body: Bayside High School defeated Flushing High School 7 to 0 at Dexter Park on Saturday before about 2,800, the Public Schools Athletic League states. The only score came in the second period. The League did not need to hear the park's record. Bayside meets Newtown on November 9.

columns.headline: Brokers' calls to Queens yesterday put at 6,240 by the Exchange
columns.body: The Queens Exchange states that it put through 6,240 calls from brokers' offices in Manhattan to Queens subscribers yesterday, a Sunday, between 9 a.m. and 11 p.m.. Superintendent Wilfred Arne states that the operators read 1,120 messages where the broker 'could not hold.'

columns.headline: Thirty-one churches keep their sermons from their systems
columns.body: The Queens Federation of Churches states that the 31 churches which switched off their house systems yesterday morning did so 'without incident' and switched them on again for the evening services. The sermons were not recorded. Attendance at the morning services was 'very large.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Cloudy. High 54. Monday. Thirty-eight points. Nobody bid 205 today.

lead.headline: The bankers don't pick up, and the Street takes a thirty-eight-point fall
lead.deck: No Whitney at the Steel post this time; nine million shares, the ticker nearly three hours behind, and at half past four the bankers come out of the Morgan office to say they never promised a floor
lead.body: On Thursday the bankers rang in and saved the afternoon. Today the Street rang them all day and got no answer. Nine million shares were sold, the average fell thirty-eight points, the worst day the Exchange has ever had, and the ticker finished nearly three hours late. At half past four the bankers came out of the Morgan office and Mr. Lamont said they had never meant to hold any particular price. The brokers heard him. Queens, at its kitchen tables, will hear the brokers tonight.

columns.headline: Ewald's tenants all pay on the line, and the landlord won't come to the phone
columns.body: Every one of the Arcade's eleven shops paid its November rent to Mr. Ewald this week, on time. He takes it to the court on Friday, which will make two thousand four hundred and seventy-two dollars. Somebody emptied the company's box again on Saturday. Nobody has rung the clerk.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Why did my broker's message come from you?'
columns.body: Madam, because he could not wait on the line and you could not be found. Yesterday the girls read eleven hundred such messages into Queens kitchens. They are told to read them exactly. Several have asked to read them gently as well. The Exchange is considering it.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? The Street is the only station on the band tonight
columns.body: The Radio Division reports WORS 1610 not heard last night. The Speaker's man on the Astoria roof reports every set in Queens tuned to the closing prices, so that a whole borough's windows said 'thirty-eight' together at seven o'clock. He says sixteen-ten would have had no audience.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Jackson Avenue, eight o'clock: three thousand at the Record's window still, waiting for prices the ticker had not reached. The Record has put a man outside with a lamp and a slate.

record.ear: Cloudy, rain by night. High 53. Low 45.

lead.headline: Stocks fall 38.3 to 260.6 on 9,210,000 shares; no bankers' support on the floor
lead.deck: Largest fall in the Exchange's history; the ticker's last price read at 6:47 p.m.; bankers meet at 4:30 p.m. and Mr. Lamont states the group was not formed to hold 'any particular level'
lead.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange fell yesterday on a volume of 9,210,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 260.6, a loss of 38.3, the largest in the Exchange's history, the Exchange states. The ticker read its last price at 6:47 p.m. The tone book enters 'broken' a second time. At 4:30 p.m. the bankers met at 23 Wall Street, and Mr. Thomas W. Lamont stated that the group did not undertake to maintain any particular level of prices.

columns.headline: Queens Exchange places 5,800 margin calls by 1 a.m.; 2,400 read by operators
columns.body: The Queens Exchange states that it placed 5,800 calls from brokers to Queens subscribers between 3 p.m. yesterday and 1 a.m. today, the operators reading 2,400 brokers' messages where the broker could not hold. Operators are asked to read 'exactly and at an even pace.'

columns.headline: Seventh postcard from Dr. Strand shows the chapel door closed from within
columns.body: Union Seminary states that it received a seventh postcard from Dr. Matthias Strand yesterday, posted at Bangor on October 14. It shows the same chapel's door, closed, taken from inside the chapel. The reverse bears the address and nothing else. The Seminary has not replied, having no address.

columns.headline: Valves at a dollar forty the six; Jamaica dealers limit sales to one box
columns.body: The Queens Radio Dealers' Association states that valves sold at a dollar forty the six yesterday and that dealers in Jamaica and Flushing limited sales to one box a customer. Eggs were unchanged at 52 cents. The Newark works state that output was raised by a quarter.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Exchange states 381 calls reporting the tone between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. today, the operators entering 'louder.'

speaker.ear: Rain. High 53. Tuesday. Sixteen million. Hold on. Hold on.

lead.headline: Sixteen million shares go out into dead air, and the ticker can't get a word in
lead.deck: The worst day there has ever been on the Exchange: everybody selling, nobody buying, the tape two and a half hours late, and the governors meeting in a room under the floor
lead.body: Sixteen and a half million shares were offered on the Exchange today, and for long stretches of the morning nobody would buy them at any price. The ticker read the closing prices at half past five. The governors met at noon in a room under the floor, so that the floor would not hear them. They did not close the Exchange. The average lost thirty points. Messengers ran up Broad Street with their collars open. The Speaker will not make a joke about it. Tomorrow, maybe.

columns.headline: The Society puts Jackson Avenue on the record for 1978
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society set its machine on the Record's sill at ten this morning and took down the crowd on Jackson Avenue all day, for 1978. Mr. Fahey says 1978 should hear it. The Speaker's man says it sounded like six thousand people holding their breath.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'How do I ring my bank?'
columns.body: Madam, ask for it by name and the girl will put you through. The savings banks of Queens say they are open and paying, every one, and the girls have been told to tell anyone who asks. Do not ring your broker. He knows. Ring your sister instead.

columns.headline: Strand's seventh card shuts the door, and he's still on the inside line
columns.body: Dr. Strand's seventh card came to Union Seminary yesterday from Bangor. The same chapel door, but shut this time, and the camera inside with it, in the dark. Nothing on the back but the address. The porter has gone back to using the front door.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Jackson Avenue, seven o'clock: the rain came on and nobody went home. The Record's man with the slate wrote the closing average, and the crowd read it, and went home then.

lead.headline: 16,410,030 shares sold; average closes at 230.1; governors meet below the floor
lead.deck: Loss of 30.6 points; the ticker's last price read at 5:32 p.m.; the tone book's clerk makes no entry; extra dividends declared by U. S. Steel and American Can after the close
lead.body: The Stock Exchange sold 16,410,030 shares yesterday, its most ever, the average closing at 230.1, a loss of 30.6, the Exchange states. The governors met at noon in a room beneath the floor and did not close the Exchange. The ticker read its last price at 5:32 p.m. The tone book's clerk made no entry at 3 p.m., stating that he 'had no word for it.' U. S. Steel and American Can declared extra dividends.

columns.headline: Queens Exchange's calls to Manhattan put at 46,800; operators kept on
columns.body: The Queens Exchange states that it put through 46,800 calls between Queens and Manhattan yesterday, the most it has recorded, and that the day's operators were kept on until 10 p.m. Superintendent Wilfred Arne states that no position was left unstaffed and that 'the board held.'

columns.headline: Senate vault's record of March 27 unclaimed in its thirty-second week
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27 containing the word 'resent' remains unclaimed in the vault at Albany in its thirty-second week. Senator Rufus Keel did not come to the vault in the hours given to his secretary.

columns.headline: Queens savings banks report deposits above withdrawals on Monday and Tuesday
columns.body: The Savings Banks Association of Queens states that deposits at its 14 member banks exceeded withdrawals on Monday and Tuesday and that no bank shortened its hours. The Corona Mutual Savings Bank states that it received 'more callers than usual, and more questions.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was heard by a Whitestone listener for about 3 minutes at 2:10 a.m. today, he states; the Radio Division did not hear it.

speaker.ear: Clearing. High 52. Wednesday. Up twenty-eight. Breathe out.

lead.headline: The Rockefellers ring in an order, and the whole Street picks up
lead.deck: The old man says he and his son have been buying sound common stocks for some days, and the average climbs twenty-eight points; the ticker almost on time
lead.body: Last night Mr. John D. Rockefeller said that he and his son had been buying sound common stocks for some days, and this morning the Street believed him. The average went up twenty-eight points on ten million shares, the best day in its history, the day after the worst. The ticker was only half an hour late. On Jackson Avenue the crowd at the Record's window was a third the size, and somebody laughed. Not much. The Exchange will shut on Friday and Saturday so that everybody can sleep.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Whitestone tunes in at ten past two, and Pike hears nothing
columns.body: A Whitestone man with a set on his porch says he heard WORS 1610 at ten past two this morning for three minutes. He will not say what it played. Mr. Pike's office says it heard nothing. The office boy has put a pin in Whitestone, on the window frame.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Is it over?'
columns.body: Sir, the operator does not know, and neither does your broker, who rang her four times today to ask. She can tell you that the calls were fewer this afternoon and that the girls had their lunch. That is the best news the board has had all week.

columns.headline: Week thirty-two: the vault keeps its hours, and the Senator's line is engaged
columns.body: Thirty-two weeks in the vault for 'resent.' Mr. Pratt has stood at the vault door at ten every day since the secretary asked the hours. The Senator has not come down. The Speaker has read 'Well. Listening. Still.' again and wishes it hadn't.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Exchange will open at noon tomorrow and close Friday and Saturday, Mr. Whitney says. The ticker has asked for nothing. It gets the week-end anyway.

lead.headline: Stocks rise 28.4 to 258.5 after Mr. Rockefeller's statement; Exchange to close
lead.deck: 10,730,000 shares; the largest gain in the Exchange's history; Exchange to open at noon today and to remain closed Friday and Saturday for the clearing of accounts
lead.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 10,730,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 258.5, a gain of 28.4, the largest in its history, the Exchange states. The rise followed Mr. John D. Rockefeller's statement that he and his son were buying common stocks. Mr. Richard Whitney announced at 1:40 p.m. that the Exchange will open at noon today and close on Friday and Saturday to allow the clearing of accounts. The tone book enters 'up.'

columns.headline: Police to keep 'ordinary watch' for Hallowe'en; house records may be heard
columns.body: The Police Department states that Queens precincts will keep an 'ordinary watch' tonight for Hallowe'en and that complaints of soaped windows and removed gates will be heard against the house record where one exists. Last year 212 complaints were made in the borough, 40 of them about gates.

columns.headline: WORS 1610 reported at Whitestone at 2:10 a.m. yesterday; not confirmed
columns.body: A Whitestone listener states that he heard the call sign WORS 1610 at 2:10 a.m. yesterday for about 3 minutes on a set on his porch. Mr. Harold Pike states that the Radio Division heard nothing at that hour and that the report is 'noted.'

columns.headline: Justice Hallam's decision on the primary records remains reserved
columns.body: The clerk of the Supreme Court at Long Island City states that Justice Moses Hallam's decision on Alderman John Feeney's application for the records of the 23 disputed primary districts remains reserved, ten days after the filing of Mr. Hollis Crane's affidavit. No date has been given.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Exchange states 594 calls reporting the tone between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. today, the operators entering 'louder.'

columns.headline: President gives Mme. Curie a draft for a gram of radium from the women of America
columns.body: President Hoover yesterday handed Mme. Marie Curie, at the National Academy of Sciences building in Washington, a draft for 50,000 dollars to buy one gram of radium for her institute at Warsaw, the gift of the women of America, Washington states. Her remarks were recorded.

columns.headline: Parents' committees to hold Hallowe'en parties at nine Queens schools
columns.body: Parents' committees will hold Hallowe'en parties at nine Queens public schools tonight from 6 p.m., the Board of Education states. Children are asked to come with an adult. Householders are reminded that soaping windows remains an offense.

columns.headline: Stocks recover part of Tuesday's loss on heavy trading; ticker late
columns.body: Stocks recovered part of Tuesday's loss yesterday on heavy trading, the Exchange states, with the ticker running late at the close. The Exchange will not open tomorrow or Saturday. Borough savings banks reported ordinary withdrawals. Pumpkins were plentiful and low at Wallabout.

columns.headline: Motor car for sale, nearly new, 1929 touring model; owner needs cash
columns.body: Five-passenger touring car, 1929 model, four thousand miles, new tires, in excellent condition. Owner requires cash this week and will consider any fair offer. May be seen at a garage on Northern Boulevard, Flushing. Box 417, this paper.

back.foot: The Borough Record, Long Island City. Corrections are printed as received.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 55. Hallowe'en. The ticker's off till Monday. Wire your gate.

lead.headline: The Exchange hangs up for the week-end, and Queens hangs out its lanterns
lead.deck: Three hours of trading from noon, then two days' rest for the tape; on the borough's stoops the pumpkins are carved, the gates are wired shut, and the children have the streets
lead.body: The Stock Exchange opened at noon today, traded three quiet hours, and shut until Monday, and the ticker went silent at ten past three like a man taking off his collar. Queens did not notice. Queens was carving. By six the stoops from Astoria to Jamaica had lanterns on them, and the children of Corona were out in sheets and burnt-cork moustaches, soaping windows. In Sunnyside a careful householder wired his gate shut. The Hum will come at one, as usual. Tonight the borough has other noises.

columns.headline: 'Danko, dog' goes out as a ghost, and P.S. 11 marks him present in spirit
columns.body: The P.S. 11 terrier went to the school's Hallowe'en party this afternoon under a pillow slip with eyeholes, sewn by nobody who will say. Mrs. Fitch says she made it. Dr. Voight says his housekeeper did. Mrs. Ahl says it is her slip. He went home in it.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? The hut cat turns her back on the Sound, and Brewer turns too
columns.body: Mr. Brewer writes from Port Washington that Sixteen-Ten the cat has turned from the water at two every morning for nineteen nights. Last night he turned with her. She was looking at the door. He says nothing came through it. He has left a saucer by it.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can a ghost come down the telephone?'
columns.body: Little girl, no. The operator connects every call into Queens herself, and she has never put a ghost through, not once, and she would know. If your telephone rings tonight and nobody speaks, it is your uncle with his hand over the mouthpiece. Tell him to stop.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Jackson Avenue, nine o'clock: the Record's window dark for the first night in a week. Two boys in sheets stood in front of it anyway, listening.
